questions.question: How should a consumer respond to a record it cannot deserialize?
questions.answer: First preserve the raw record and identify whether the issue is malformed bytes, an unknown schema, a missing registry dependency or an incompatible consumer rollout. Blindly retrying deterministic bad data blocks the partition without making progress. A safe quarantine path should capture topic, partition, offset, key, headers and a protected payload representation, then apply an explicit commit policy so the poison item is not silently skipped. Validate registry connectivity and compatibility separately from business handler errors. I would deploy compatible consumers before producers and test old retained messages as well as newly emitted records.

followups.q: Is every deserialization exception permanent?
followups.a: No. A missing external schema service may be transient; distinguish infrastructure failures from invalid payloads.

followups.q: Can a consumer commit past one malformed record safely?
followups.a: Only after the record is durably quarantined and the business ordering consequences are accepted.

questions.trap: Logging an error and advancing the offset without retaining enough data to diagnose or replay.
verify: [VERIFY: Check serializer/registry exception behavior and schema compatibility policy for the selected client.]

questions.question: How should a Kafka client recover from a temporary network partition?
questions.answer: A network break can leave request outcomes ambiguous, interrupt metadata refresh and trigger consumer group changes. Use the client's reconnection and retry behavior with bounded request and delivery deadlines, and make producer and consumer work safe to repeat. Application-level retries should use backoff and a deadline rather than multiplying unbounded retries beneath library retries. On recovery, confirm metadata refresh, successful sends or reconciled outcomes, partition ownership and lag drain. I would distinguish DNS, routing, firewall, TLS and broker failures from a generic timeout using client logs and network telemetry, without logging secrets.

followups.q: Should retry be layered in both client and application?
followups.a: Only with coordinated budgets; nested unlimited retries can amplify load and exceed the request deadline.

followups.q: Does connectivity recovery prove a timed-out send failed?
followups.a: No. The send may have reached the broker; reconcile using stable event identity.

questions.trap: Retrying every timeout immediately and assuming the original operation had no effect.
verify: [VERIFY: Review networking, TLS and retry configuration for the deployed Kafka client and cluster.]

questions.question: What can RabbitMQ flow control or blocked publishing indicate, and how should producers react?
questions.answer: The broker may slow or block publishers when memory, disk or other resource thresholds are reached, or when a connection is otherwise constrained. The producer must not treat a successful local method call as proof that the broker can accept unlimited work. Observe connection-blocked notifications, confirm latency, broker alarms and queue growth; then apply bounded backpressure to callers or durably retain work upstream. Blind retry loops can increase pressure. I would identify the specific broker alarm, protect process memory, and verify that the client resumes cleanly after unblocking without losing or duplicating ambiguous publications.

followups.q: Should a producer open unlimited connections when blocked?
followups.a: No. That can amplify resource pressure; follow the broker/client recovery design and bound concurrency.

followups.q: What must be checked after unblock?
followups.a: Outstanding confirm outcomes, application backlog, duplicate handling and broker resource recovery.

questions.trap: Treating broker flow control as a transient warning to ignore while continuing unbounded sends.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify blocked-connection callbacks and alarm behavior for the RabbitMQ client and server version.]

questions.question: How do you explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once processing without overclaiming?
questions.answer: At-most-once can lose work but avoids retry duplicates when progress is advanced before the effect. At-least-once favors retry after uncertain completion and therefore requires duplicate-safe effects. Exactly-once is meaningful only after naming the boundary: Kafka transactions can atomically coordinate supported Kafka output and input offsets, but an external database or HTTP call is not automatically enrolled. I would state the failure windows, transaction boundary, idempotency key and recovery behavior. For external effects, an inbox/outbox or transactional state change can help, but its guarantees depend on the database transaction and relay design.

followups.q: Which mode is usually chosen for durable business processing?
followups.a: Often at-least-once with idempotent effects, because retries avoid silently discarding work.

followups.q: Does an idempotent handler make transport exactly-once?
followups.a: No; it makes repeated effects converge for a defined identity, while delivery can still repeat.

questions.trap: Using exactly-once as a product-wide promise without defining which systems and operations are included.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify transactional processing limits and client isolation settings for the Kafka release in use.]

questions.question: How can an application avoid losing a Kafka event when its database transaction succeeds?
questions.answer: Writing the database and publishing to Kafka as two independent operations creates a crash window: one may succeed while the other does not. An outbox records the event in the same database transaction as the business change; a separate relay publishes pending rows and marks progress only after broker confirmation. The relay can still publish duplicates if it crashes between confirmation and marking, so consumers need event identity and idempotency. I would define retention, ordering per entity, relay retries and outbox cleanup, then monitor oldest unpublished age. This is a pattern, not an automatic distributed transaction.

followups.q: Does outbox guarantee only one Kafka record?
followups.a: Not by itself; a relay may publish again after an ambiguous confirmation or crash.

followups.q: What is the main atomic boundary?
followups.a: The business write and outbox insert share the database transaction; Kafka publication happens later.

questions.trap: Claiming a transactional outbox removes duplicates or requires no relay recovery design.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; included as a messaging handoff contract rather than a general distributed-systems design question.

questions.question: Why should a RabbitMQ consumer assume a message can be delivered more than once?
questions.answer: A consumer can complete a side effect and fail before its acknowledgement reaches the broker, leaving the delivery eligible for redelivery. Connection loss, consumer cancellation and broker recovery can also make the outcome uncertain. The broker's delivery tag is scoped to a channel delivery, not a durable business idempotency key. Include a stable event identifier and record completed handling in the same database transaction as the business update, or make the operation naturally idempotent. I would test crashes on both sides of the acknowledgement and define how duplicates are observable without repeating non-idempotent actions.

followups.q: Can a delivery tag deduplicate across reconnects?
followups.a: No. It identifies a delivery within its channel context, not a permanent message identity.

followups.q: What if the business operation is naturally idempotent?
followups.a: Then repeating the same state-setting action can be safe, but verify that all side effects share that property.

questions.trap: Assuming a broker delivery tag or manual ack guarantees the business command runs exactly once.

questions.question: Why do RabbitMQ applications use channels, and how should they handle channel-level failure?
questions.answer: A connection is the network session to the broker, while channels multiplex protocol operations over that connection and maintain delivery and acknowledgement context. A protocol exception can close one channel without necessarily closing the whole connection. Recovery must recreate channel state, declarations, bindings, consumers and confirm tracking as appropriate; unacknowledged deliveries may be redelivered. Avoid sharing a channel unsafely across concurrent threads unless the client explicitly supports it. I would distinguish connection recovery from channel recovery in metrics and logs, and design callbacks to be idempotent so repeated topology setup is safe.

followups.q: Does a channel error always close the connection?
followups.a: Not necessarily; scope depends on the protocol error and client/server behavior.

followups.q: Can all application threads share one channel?
followups.a: Follow the client library's concurrency contract; use isolated channels when concurrent protocol operations are unsafe.

questions.trap: Rebuilding only the socket and assuming consumers, confirms and channel-scoped state came back automatically.
verify: [VERIFY: Check channel thread-safety and automatic-recovery behavior for the exact RabbitMQ client release.]

questions.question: What should a consumer do with in-flight RabbitMQ deliveries when it is cancelled or shutting down?
questions.answer: Stop accepting new deliveries, then finish or safely cancel work already received within a bounded shutdown deadline. Acknowledge only tasks whose side effects reached the intended durable boundary; leave unfinished work unacknowledged so broker redelivery can recover it, while ensuring the channel is closed according to the client lifecycle. If a task completed but its acknowledgement is uncertain, the handler must tolerate redelivery. I would coordinate shutdown with the service's deployment grace period, cap in-flight concurrency, and test termination during database work and during acknowledgement to expose both loss and duplicate windows.

followups.q: Should shutdown acknowledge all deliveries to finish quickly?
followups.a: No. Acknowledging incomplete effects can permanently lose work.

followups.q: What if the process deadline expires?
followups.a: Allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered and ensure repeated effects are safe.

questions.trap: Treating a cancellation notification as proof all application tasks stopped or completed.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify cancellation callback and channel-close behavior for the deployed RabbitMQ client version.]

questions.question: What isolation does a RabbitMQ virtual host provide, and what does it not isolate?
questions.answer: A virtual host provides a namespace for exchanges, queues, bindings and related permissions, allowing applications or environments to avoid name collisions and apply separate access rules. It is not a separate broker process or guaranteed resource boundary: CPU, memory, disk, cluster availability and some operational limits are shared. Credentials and permissions must be scoped to the intended vhost, and clients must connect to the correct one. I would use vhosts to organize trust and lifecycle boundaries while still using broker-level capacity controls and monitoring to prevent one tenant from exhausting shared resources.

followups.q: Does a vhost isolate disk or CPU?
followups.a: Not as an independent physical broker; infrastructure resources remain shared.

followups.q: Why is naming the correct vhost important?
followups.a: A client can authenticate successfully yet declare or consume from a different namespace than intended.

questions.trap: Treating vhost separation as complete resource or failure isolation.
verify: [VERIFY: Confirm vhost permission and resource-limit behavior against the deployed RabbitMQ release and configuration.]

questions.question: What does TLS protect for a RabbitMQ connection, and what authorization remains necessary?
questions.answer: TLS protects confidentiality and integrity of the transport and, when configured for mutual authentication, can authenticate a client certificate to the broker. The broker must still map the authenticated identity to permissions for the intended virtual host, exchanges, queues and operations. A trusted server certificate must be validated by the client; disabling hostname or chain checks defeats important peer authentication. Certificate rotation, protocol versions and cipher choices should follow the organization's supported policy. I would test both trusted and rejected peers, least-privilege authorization and renewal before expiry, and avoid logging private key material.

followups.q: Does encryption grant access to a queue?
followups.a: No. Authentication and authorization determine the permitted operations separately.

followups.q: Is accepting any server certificate safe inside a private network?
followups.a: No. It removes peer identity validation and leaves the connection vulnerable to impersonation.

questions.trap: Equating encrypted transport with authenticated, authorized messaging.
verify: [VERIFY: Check TLS listener, client-authentication and certificate-mapping configuration for the deployed RabbitMQ release.]

questions.question: How do clustering, federation and shovel solve different RabbitMQ connectivity needs?
questions.answer: A cluster groups broker nodes into one broker deployment with shared operational topology and node-failure behavior determined by queue type. Federation connects exchanges or queues across broker boundaries with looser coupling, while a shovel moves messages between endpoints through a configured forwarding process. These choices differ in latency, autonomy, network partition behavior, topology ownership and duplicate risk. None should be treated as a magical global queue. I would begin with the failure and administrative boundaries, then verify delivery semantics, loop prevention, credentials and recovery behavior for the selected feature and RabbitMQ version.

followups.q: Does clustering automatically create a globally replicated queue?
followups.a: No; queue type and placement determine data replication and availability.

followups.q: What should a cross-broker bridge monitor?
followups.a: Source and destination rates, link health, backlog age, retries and duplicate or loop conditions.

questions.trap: Using clustering, federation and shovel as interchangeable terms for replication.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify current supported feature behavior and queue-type interactions for the deployed RabbitMQ release.]

questions.question: How should correlation and trace context travel through asynchronous messaging?
questions.answer: Propagate a stable correlation identifier and supported trace context in agreed message metadata, then extract it when the consumer starts a new processing span. A message may be delayed, retried or handled by another process, so logs should include event identity and broker coordinates without exposing payload secrets. Trace context is diagnostic input, not authorization, and should be validated and bounded. Retries may create multiple spans for one event; distinguish event identity from individual processing attempts. I would test propagation across producer, broker and consumer and ensure sampling does not erase operational metrics needed for queue health.

followups.q: Can a trace ID authorize access?
followups.a: No. Observability metadata is not an authenticated permission claim.

followups.q: Should every retry reuse the same trace span?
followups.a: No; preserve causal linkage but represent each processing attempt appropriately in the tracing model.

questions.trap: Treating a caller-supplied correlation header as trusted identity or logging full sensitive payloads.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify the tracing library's messaging propagation convention and broker instrumentation support in use.]

questions.question: What happens when a Kafka application changes its consumer group ID?
questions.answer: A new group ID has independent committed offsets, so it typically behaves like a new subscriber and applies the configured initial-position policy rather than resuming the old group's progress. That can replay retained data, start later than expected or create a second full processing stream. The old group metadata remains subject to retention. I would treat group ID changes as data migrations: document intended replay, check idempotent side effects and capacity, and coordinate deployment so old and new groups do not unintentionally compete or duplicate business actions.

followups.q: Does a renamed group inherit the old offset automatically?
followups.a: No. Offset transfer requires an explicit supported migration; group IDs do not imply shared progress.

followups.q: Why might a new group be intentional?
followups.a: It can create an independent subscription or controlled replay, if duplicate effects and load are handled.

questions.trap: Changing the group name as a harmless deployment detail.
verify: [VERIFY: Confirm offset-reset behavior and group migration tooling for the deployed Kafka release.]

questions.question: What topic-level choices should be agreed before a production event stream is created?
questions.answer: Define the owner, event contract, key and ordering domain, expected throughput, partition and replication strategy, retention or compaction policy, access controls and schema evolution rules. Establish naming and environment conventions so test data or one team's consumer cannot collide with production. Document who can create or alter topics and how changes are reviewed and rolled out. These settings affect replay, storage, availability and downstream parallelism, so defaults should not silently become the contract. I would automate validated provisioning and review actual broker policies, while leaving capacity numbers as measured assumptions that need monitoring.

followups.q: Why document the partition key?
followups.a: It encodes the ordering and distribution decision that consumers may depend on.

followups.q: Should applications create topics automatically?
followups.a: Only under a controlled policy; implicit creation can hide naming and configuration errors.

questions.trap: Creating a production topic with defaults and no owner, retention, access or replay decision.
verify: [VERIFY: Verify broker auto-creation and topic-policy enforcement for the target environment.]

questions.question: How would you choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ for a new asynchronous workflow?
questions.answer: Start from the message contract and recovery need. Kafka is a partitioned retained log suited to replayable streams, independent consumer groups and high-throughput ordered partitions. RabbitMQ routes deliveries through exchanges and queues, with acknowledgements, queue-oriented work distribution and flexible routing. Either can support durable asynchronous processing, and either can be misconfigured. Compare per-entity ordering, replay window, consumer behavior, routing, latency, operations, retention cost and team expertise. I would model failure and duplicate handling before choosing, then validate load and recovery on the intended topology instead of selecting by a generic throughput slogan.

followups.q: Is Kafka only for analytics?
followups.a: No. It can support operational event streams when its partitioned-log and retention model fits.

followups.q: Is RabbitMQ only for request-response?
followups.a: No. It supports asynchronous work queues and routed messaging; select features from the needed contract.

questions.trap: Claiming one broker is universally faster, more reliable or a drop-in substitute for the other.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 8.1 (Impetus, Randstad).

questions.question: Producers are faster than consumers. How do you handle growing lag?
questions.answer: First measure consumer lag with a tool such as Burrow or the Kafka exporter, and alert on it. Scale consumers horizontally up to the number of partitions in Kafka, adding partitions if you are at the limit; in RabbitMQ add competing consumers. Increase per-consumer throughput with concurrency settings, batch listeners and bulk database writes, and remove per-message round trips, taking care of ordering. Apply back-pressure with bounded queues, prefetch limits and producer throttling. Watch max.poll.interval.ms, because a slow handler triggers rebalances that worsen lag. If consumers are faster than producers, the consumer simply waits in poll() using no CPU, and idle instances can be scaled down, for example with lag-based autoscaling.

followups.q: Why does adding consumers beyond the partition count not help?
followups.a: Each partition is read by one consumer in a group, so extra consumers sit idle.

followups.q: How can a slow handler worsen lag?
followups.a: If it exceeds max.poll.interval.ms the consumer is removed and a rebalance pauses processing for the group.

questions.trap: Adding consumers without checking the partition count or why the handler is slow.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 8.2 (Impetus). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S10-016, JH-S19-055.

questions.question: What is a Kafka offset, and how do committed offsets and lag relate?
questions.answer: An offset is a record's sequential position within a partition, and a consumer group tracks its progress per topic and partition. The current position is the next record to read, the committed offset is the last acknowledged position stored in the internal __consumer_offsets topic, and the log-end offset is the newest record; lag is the log-end offset minus the committed offset. Auto-commit on a timer can commit before processing finishes and lose messages, so committing manually after processing gives at-least-once delivery. auto.offset.reset (earliest, latest or none) decides where to start when no committed offset exists. A consumer can seek to an offset or timestamp to replay records.

followups.q: Why can auto-commit lose messages?
followups.a: It may commit offsets for records whose processing has not finished, so a crash skips them.

followups.q: What does auto.offset.reset control?
followups.a: Where a group starts when it has no valid committed offset: earliest, latest or fail with none.

questions.trap: Describing offsets as global message ids. They are per partition and meaningful only within it.
